subject: mathematics
question_text: Let f: A→B and g: B→A be defined by f = {(1, a), (2, c), (4, d), (3, b)} and g⁻¹ = {(2, a), (4, b), (1, c), (3, d)}. Verify that (gof)⁻¹ = f⁻¹og⁻¹.

mark_split.label: Write g from the given g⁻¹

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, FAST TRACK IPE for Jr. Students — Mathematics-IA (2026-27 edition), chapter 2 FUNCTIONS, Short Answer question 2, book p.16. Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. ⚠ THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the Mathematics-IA volume prints no per-step mark allocation on any answer. The 1+1+1+1 shape is the one this bank uses for a Maths-1A Section B question; here each mark buys one of the four objects the student has to build in order — g, then gof, then the two reversed sets, then the comparison. Paper position: Maths-1A Section B prints 8 short answer questions, the student answers any 6, and each carries 4 marks (2026-27 pattern). The source book's own MODEL PAPER-IA puts this question at Q11, Section II, which is that paper's single Functions short-answer slot; that is the book's claim about its own model paper, not a printed board appearance, so appearances[] is empty. ON THE STEM: the printed stem never names A and B. They are read off the pairs as A = {1, 2, 3, 4} and B = {a, b, c, d}, which is the only reading under which f: A→B and g: B→A are both defined; the stem is well posed on that reading and has not been altered. Note also that g is supplied through g⁻¹, so the first thing the answer has to do is produce g. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

recall_prompt: Say how you would verify this — what you have to build from the given g⁻¹, and what you compare at the end.

steps.label: Write g from the given g⁻¹
steps.margin_note: One of the four marks. The question hands you g⁻¹, not g. Reverse its four pairs first, and check that the result has domain B.
steps.memory_tip: g is not given. Reverse the pairs of g⁻¹ first, and check the domain comes out as B.
lines: Reverse each pair to get g: B→A.

recall.must_convey: That g itself is not given, so its four pairs are obtained by reversing g⁻¹, giving g = {(a,2), (b,4), (c,1), (d,3)} with domain B.

g is a two b four c one d three

steps.why: g itself is not given, only g⁻¹. Every later step needs g, so writing it out first stops the composition being done with the wrong function.
common_mistakes: Using g⁻¹ in place of g when working out gof.
Writing g with domain A instead of B.

steps.label: Find gof
steps.margin_note: The second mark. f first, then g. Each element of A comes back to an element of A, so gof runs from A to A.
steps.memory_tip: f carries 1 to a, then g carries a to 2. Follow one element the whole way before starting the next.

recall.must_convey: That gof applies f then g, so gof = {(1,2), (2,1), (3,4), (4,3)}, a function from A to A.
accept: one goes to a then to two, two goes to c then to one, three goes to b then to four, four goes to d then to three
g o f is one two two one three four four three
f first then g so the composition runs from A back to A
mundu f taruvata g apply cheste gof vasthundi
each element of A comes back to an element of A
reject: reverse the pairs of g inverse
g acts first and then f
both sides hold the same four pairs

steps.why: gof takes A to B by f and then B to A by g, so gof is a function from A to A. Working one element at a time is the whole method for a finite function.
common_mistakes: Pairing the image of f with the wrong first coordinate.

steps.label: Write (gof)⁻¹ and f⁻¹
steps.margin_note: The third mark. Reverse the four pairs of gof, then reorder them by first coordinate so the comparison at the end is easy. Write f⁻¹ here too, because the last step needs it.
steps.memory_tip: Reverse every pair, then reorder by the first coordinate. Reordering does not change the set.
lines: gof is a bijection, so reverse every pair:
Reverse the pairs of f as well:

recall.must_convey: That reversing the pairs of gof gives (gof)⁻¹ = {(1,2), (2,1), (3,4), (4,3)}, and that f⁻¹ = {(a,1), (c,2), (b,3), (d,4)}.

one goes to a then to two
the two sides agree at every element

steps.why: gof happens to send 1 to 2 and 2 back to 1, so its inverse comes out as the same set of pairs. That is a property of these particular numbers, not a rule, and it is worth checking rather than reading as a slip.
common_mistakes: Writing (gof)⁻¹ = gof without reversing the pairs first.
Reversing only some of the four pairs.

steps.label: Form f⁻¹og⁻¹ and compare
steps.margin_note: The fourth mark. Use the given g⁻¹ as it stands here — it does not need reversing again. Compare the four pairs with line (1) one at a time.
steps.memory_tip: The given g⁻¹ is used unchanged in this step. Only g needed reversing, back in the first step.
lines: f⁻¹og⁻¹ means g⁻¹ first, then f⁻¹.
This is the same set of four pairs as (1).

recall.must_convey: That f⁻¹og⁻¹ applies g⁻¹ first, giving {(1,2), (2,1), (3,4), (4,3)}, which is the same set as (gof)⁻¹, so the two are equal.
accept: g inverse acts first so one goes to c then to two, two goes to a then to one, three goes to d then to four, four goes to b then to three
f inverse o g inverse is one two two one three four four three
both sides hold the same four pairs so they are equal

the composition is done in the reversed order and it matches

steps.why: Both sides are functions from A to A, so the check is only whether the four values match. The reversed order f⁻¹og⁻¹, and not g⁻¹of⁻¹, is what the result states.
common_mistakes: Working out g⁻¹of⁻¹ instead of f⁻¹og⁻¹.
Using g instead of g⁻¹ in the composition.
